lesson.title: Two Shared Pairs: Building Stronger, Shorter Bonds
lesson.summary: A double bond forms when two atoms share two full pairs of electrons instead of one, producing a bond that is shorter and stronger than a single bond and is often the tool a Lewis structure needs to complete a central atom's octet.
lesson.body:
A double bond is what happens when two atoms share not one but two full pairs of electrons between them, four electrons total, drawn in a Lewis structure as two parallel lines connecting the atoms instead of one. It is the natural next step beyond the single bond: wherever one shared pair alone would leave an atom short of a complete octet, converting a neighboring lone pair into a second shared pair between the same two atoms can close that gap without needing to add or remove any electrons from the total count.

Oxygen gas, O2, is a clear example of exactly when this upgrade is necessary. Each oxygen atom contributes six valence electrons, for a total of 12. Connecting the two oxygens with a single bond and giving each atom three lone pairs would use all 12 electrons, but it would leave each oxygen with only seven electrons around it, one short of an octet. Converting one of those lone pairs on each oxygen into a second shared pair instead, forming O=O, fixes the shortfall: each oxygen atom now has one double bond, counted as four electrons toward its octet, plus two remaining lone pairs, four more electrons, for a complete octet of eight on each atom, using the same 12 electrons as before, just redistributed.

Carbon dioxide, CO2, needs the same trick applied twice. Carbon contributes four valence electrons and each oxygen contributes six, for a total of 16. With carbon in the center bonded to both oxygens, single bonds alone would leave carbon with only four electrons, badly short of an octet, and each oxygen with seven. Forming a double bond to each oxygen instead, O=C=O, gives carbon two double bonds, eight electrons total, a complete octet with no lone pairs needed on carbon at all, while each oxygen keeps two lone pairs alongside its one double bond, again reaching eight. This is also a case where the earlier procedure for Lewis structures, checking the central atom's octet last and upgrading single bonds when it comes up short, does exactly the right thing automatically.

Ethylene, C2H4, shows a double bond between two carbon atoms in an organic molecule. Each carbon contributes four valence electrons and each of the four hydrogens contributes one, for 12 electrons total. A C=C double bond accounts for four of those electrons, and four C-H single bonds, two on each carbon, account for the remaining eight, with no lone pairs anywhere in the molecule, since every electron is already accounted for in a bond and both carbons reach a full octet through two C-H bonds plus one double bond.

Because a double bond packs two shared pairs of electrons into the space between the same two nuclei, the electrostatic attraction pulling those nuclei together is considerably stronger, and the equilibrium bond length is noticeably shorter, than what a single bond between the identical pair of atoms would produce. A carbon-carbon double bond has a length of about 134 picometers, compared to about 154 picometers for a carbon-carbon single bond, and a bond energy of about 614 kilojoules per mole, compared to about 347 kilojoules per mole for the single bond. Note that a double bond is stronger than a single bond, but it is not simply twice as strong, since the second shared pair does not reinforce the bond as efficiently as the first one did, a detail that becomes relevant once triple bonds and overall bond order enter the picture in later chapters.
